commitResults.messageTitle: Rename chatbot to Ted and greet the user on startup
commitResults.messageBody:
Rename the Duke class to Ted (with a matching ASCII banner) so the
project uses its own product name rather than the template's default,
updating both READMEs to match.

Implement the Level-0 requirement: the chatbot now prints its banner,
greets the user, and immediately says goodbye, with each section
separated by a horizontal line. The divider is extracted into a
printLine() helper rather than repeating the literal string, since
every future command response will need the same separator.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: AGENTS.md: Fill in the student profile
commitResults.messageBody:
Replace the [to be filled] placeholders with the actual experience level
and IDE, so AI assistants working in this repo can pitch explanations at
the right level instead of guessing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Ted.java: Echo user commands until 'bye'
commitResults.messageBody:
Ted printed a greeting and exited immediately, so there was no way to
interact with it. Add a read-print loop so the user can enter commands.

Each line entered is echoed back between horizontal rules, and the
command 'bye' ends the conversation. Input is trimmed so that stray
whitespace does not stop 'bye' from matching, and the loop also stops on
end-of-input so that piping a script into the program exits cleanly
rather than throwing NoSuchElementException.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Ted.java: Add task storage and the list command
commitResults.messageBody:
Ted previously echoed each input straight back and forgot it. He now
remembers what the user types and can recall it on demand:

* Non-command input is stored and acknowledged with "added: <task>".
* The "list" command prints the stored tasks, numbered from 1.

Tasks are held in a fixed-size String[100] with a separate taskCount,
which is sufficient because this increment caps the task count at 100.
An ArrayList would be the natural replacement once that cap is lifted,
but the array keeps the code simple for now.

Adding beyond the 100-task limit reports the failure instead of writing
past the end of the array, so a dropped task is never silent, and "list"
on an empty task list says so rather than printing an empty response.

Also fixed the farewell, which printed with only a trailing separator
line, so that it is bracketed on both sides like every other response.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Ted.java: Add the mark command
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks previously had no state beyond their description, so there was no
way to record progress. A parallel boolean[] now tracks the done status
of each task, and "mark <number>" sets it.

The list output changes to show a status icon per task ("1.[X] read
book"), which is the format the later increments build on.

A mistyped task number is a normal part of using a chatbot, so
parseTaskIndex reports missing, non-numeric, and out-of-range numbers
instead of letting the exception escape and end the conversation.

Keeping the description and its done status in two parallel arrays is
deliberately awkward at this step; the next commits introduce a Task
class that bundles them together.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Ted.java: Add the unmark command
commitResults.messageBody:
A task marked done by mistake could not be corrected without restarting
Ted. "unmark <number>" now reverses the done status.

Marking and unmarking differ only in the flag they store and the wording
they print, so both route through one setTaskDone method rather than
duplicating the task-number lookup and its error handling.

"unmark" is tested before "mark" when dispatching, because "unmark 2"
would otherwise have to be distinguished from a mark command by a more
fragile check.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a Task class to represent tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
A task's description and its done status were held in two parallel
arrays, which only stayed in step because every write updated both by
hand. A Task object now owns both, so a task cannot lose its status.

Task also overrides toString, which moves the display format next to the
data it formats and lets a task be printed wherever it is needed. This
replaces Ted's formatTask helper, which had to reach into both arrays.

Task is a separate file rather than a nested class because the later
increments give it subclasses for the different kinds of task.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Todo, Deadline and Event task types
commitResults.messageBody:
Every task was the same shape, so a due date or a time span had to be
buried in the description as plain text. Ted now understands three
commands that create three kinds of task, each shown with its own type
icon: todo, deadline (/by) and event (/from, /to).

Task becomes abstract and gains an abstract getTypeIcon, because a task
with no kind is no longer something the user can create. Deadline and
Event extend toString by calling super and appending their own detail,
so the shared "[icon][status] description" format is defined once.

Dates stay free text, as this increment allows; "no idea :-p" is as
valid as "Sunday". Converting them to real dates comes later.

Adding a task now reports the task and the resulting task count, which
is what the later delete command will echo too.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Handle invalid user input with a TedException
commitResults.messageBody:
Bad input was handled inconsistently: some cases printed a message from
deep inside a helper, some returned a sentinel -1 the caller had to
remember to check, and an empty todo was stored as a blank task.

Every recoverable problem is now reported by throwing a TedException,
caught in one place in the main loop. Detecting code says what went
wrong, the loop decides how to show it, and no failure can slip past a
forgotten sentinel check. The exception is checked, because each of
these is a normal part of a conversation rather than a bug.

Messages name the specific problem and show a working example, so the
user can correct the command without consulting a guide.

Dispatch now splits the command word from its argument instead of using
startsWith, which also fixes "todos something" being silently accepted
as a todo named "s something".

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add the delete command and store tasks in an ArrayList
commitResults.messageBody:
A task added by mistake could not be removed. "delete <number>" now
removes one and echoes it, since after it is gone the user has no other
way to confirm the number they typed was the one they meant.

Deleting from the fixed-size array would have meant shifting every later
task down by hand and keeping a separate count in step, so tasks move to
an ArrayList, which closes the gap itself and reports its own size. The
100-task cap and its "list is full" error disappear with it, as the list
grows as needed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Represent commands with an enum instead of String constants
commitResults.messageBody:
The command words were eight loose String constants matched by a switch
over raw strings, so a typo in a constant or a case label would compile
and only show up as a command that silently stopped working. The list of
keywords in the "I don't recognise that" message was a ninth copy that
had to be edited by hand whenever a command was added, and had already
drifted once.

A Command enum now owns each keyword and looks it up in one place, so
the compiler checks every use, the switch reads as a list of commands
rather than of strings, and the message shown to a confused user is
built from the commands themselves.

Blank input is now ignored rather than answered with a complaint about
an empty command word.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Persist tasks between application runs
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks exist only in memory, so exiting Ted loses the user's task list.

Let's load tasks during startup and save after each list mutation. Store
them in a human-readable format, with escaping so free-form text can
round-trip without changing field boundaries.

Ignore generated class and runtime data files so local runs do not
pollute commits.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-Level-7 into master
Store deadline and event times as date-times
commitResults.messageBody:
Deadline and Event keep their times as free text, so Ted cannot tell
"2/12/2019 1800" from "no idea :-p".

That rules out anything that reasons about time, such as ordering tasks
or listing what is due on a given day, and lets nonsense through.

Let's store the times as java.time.LocalDateTime, read in d/M/yyyy HHmm
form and shown back as "2 Dec 2019, 6:00 pm". Times Ted cannot read are
reported as a TedException, and an event that ends before it starts is
now rejected.

The save file uses ISO-8601 rather than the display format, so it stays
unambiguous and independent of how Ted happens to print dates.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-Level-8 into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Brings in Level 8: deadlines and events store their times as
LocalDateTime instead of free text.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract Ui, TaskList and Storage responsibilities
commitResults.messageBody:
Ted prints the banner, reads the keyboard, holds the task list, checks
task numbers and writes the save file.

One class holding all of that means a change to any one of them edits
the same file, and none of it can be exercised without a terminal.

Let's split those responsibilities out:
* Ui owns the Scanner and every System.out
* TaskList owns the tasks and the rule that a task number must point at
  a real task
* Storage takes its file path from the constructor and reports failures
  as a TedException instead of printing them

Storage taking a path rather than hard-coding one lets a later test
point it at a scratch file instead of the real save file.

commitResults.messageTitle: Parser: read user input into Command objects
commitResults.messageBody:
Ted routes every command itself, through a switch that calls one private
method per command word, and those methods do the reading and the work
in one go.

Every new command therefore means another branch in that switch and
another method on an already large class, and nothing that reads user
input can be tested apart from the code that acts on it.

Let's,
* add a Command class with one subclass per kind of command, each
  carrying out its own work through execute(tasks, ui, storage)
* move all input reading into a new Parser, which returns the Command
  the user asked for
* rename the old Command enum to CommandType, since it now names the
  kinds of command rather than being one

Splitting reading from doing means a command is only built once its
details make sense, so the command classes need no input checking, and
Parser can be tested without a keyboard or a save file.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-MoreOOP into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Brings in A-MoreOOP: Ui, TaskList, Storage, Parser and the Command
classes are now separate, leaving Ted to wire them together.

commitResults.messageTitle: Organise the classes into packages
commitResults.messageBody:
All seventeen classes sit in the default package, so src/main/java is a
flat list in which nothing says which classes belong together.

The default package also cannot be imported from elsewhere, and the list
only gets harder to read as more classes are added.

Let's group them into three packages under src/main/java:
* ted for the app itself: Ted, Ui, Parser, Storage, TedException
* ted.task for the tasks and the list holding them
* ted.command for the commands and the keywords naming them

Splitting by role rather than keeping one ted package makes the
boundaries between talking, storing and doing visible in the folder
structure. Task.SAVE_FIELD_SEPARATOR becomes public because Storage,
which splits save lines on it, now sits outside ted.task.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-Packages into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Brings in A-Packages: the classes are grouped into ted, ted.task and
ted.command.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge add-gradle-support into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Brings in the Gradle wrapper and build.gradle, so the project can be
built, run and tested with one command on any machine.

commitResults.messageTitle: build.gradle: Point Gradle at this project
commitResults.messageBody:
The build file merged in from add-gradle-support names seedu.duke.Duke
as the main class and duke.jar as the JAR to build.

Neither exists here, so `gradlew run` fails on a project whose entry
point is ted.Ted.

Let's set mainClass to ted.Ted and the shadowJar name to ted.jar.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for Parser, TaskList, Storage and Task
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing in the project is covered by an automated test, so every change
has to be checked by typing commands at the chatbot and reading what
comes back.

That is slow, easy to skip, and quietly misses the cases a person would
not think to type, such as a save file someone edited by hand.

Let's add 57 JUnit tests over the four classes whose failures would hurt
most:
* ParserTest, since Parser is where malformed input is caught
* TaskListTest, for the bounds checking behind every task number
* StorageTest, for the save-and-load round trip, writing in a @TempDir
  so the tests never touch the real save file
* TaskTest, for the display and save formats

Writing them turned up one bug: the default date resolver silently
rounded 31/2/2019 down to 28 Feb, so Ted accepted a date the user could
not have meant. Parser now uses the strict resolver, which rejects it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-JUnit into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Brings in A-JUnit: 57 tests over Parser, TaskList, Storage and Task, plus
the strict date resolver those tests prompted.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document the packages and the remaining overrides
commitResults.messageBody:
Most classes and methods carry a Javadoc header, but the three packages
have none, several overrides in ted.command and ted.task are undocumented,
and `gradlew javadoc` reports five warnings about default constructors.

A reader opening the generated docs therefore meets three unexplained
packages, and the warnings hide any real problem that appears later.

Let's,
* add package-info.java for ted, ted.task and ted.command, each saying
  what the package is for and how its classes fit together
* document the execute() overrides, isExit() and the getTypeIcon()
  overrides
* give Ui, Command, ListCommand and ExitCommand documented constructors,
  and make Parser's private since it is used through static methods only

`gradlew javadoc` now runs clean.

commitResults.messageTitle: Follow the SE-EDU Java coding standard
commitResults.messageBody:
The project has no written coding standard, so nothing says which
conventions the code follows or which ones new code should follow.

Without that, style drifts as the code grows, and neither a reader nor an
AI assistant working in this repository has anything to check against.

Let's adopt the SE-EDU Java coding standard at the intermediate level:
* record it in AGENTS.md, along with the SE-EDU Git commit conventions,
  so future code and commits are held to both
* move the two trailing end-of-line comments onto their own line above
  the code they explain

The rest of the code already complies: a sweep for tabs, over-long lines,
wildcard imports, misgrouped imports and brace-less bodies found nothing
else to change.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a find command
commitResults.messageBody:
A user with a long list can only look for a task by reading the whole
list and picking it out by eye.

That gets harder with every task added, and the list is the only view
Ted offers.

Let's add `find <keyword>`, which shows the tasks whose description
contains the keyword:

    find book
    Here are the matching tasks in your list:
    1.[T][X] read book
    2.[D][X] return book (by: 6 Jun 2026, 6:00 pm)

The search ignores case and matches part of a word, since a user
searching for "book" should not have to remember whether they typed
"Book" or "bookshop" when adding the task.

The matches are numbered from 1 as their own list, so those numbers are
not the ones to pass to mark or delete.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-JavaDoc into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Brings in A-JavaDoc: package-info for the three packages, headers on the
remaining overrides, and a warning-free `gradlew javadoc`.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-CodingStandard into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Brings in A-CodingStandard: the SE-EDU Java coding standard and Git commit
conventions are recorded in AGENTS.md, and the code complies.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-Level-9 into master
commitResults.messageBody:
Brings in Level 9: a find command that shows the tasks whose description
contains a keyword.

commitResults.messageTitle: FindCommand: Add the missing header comment
commitResults.messageBody:
FindCommand was written on branch-Level-9, in parallel with the JavaDoc
pass on branch-A-JavaDoc, so its execute() override missed that pass.

Every other execute() override carries a one-line header saying what the
command does and whether it saves.

Let's give FindCommand the same, so the command classes read alike.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add CheckStyle to the build
commitResults.messageBody:
The coding standard this project follows is only checked by eye at
the moment. Style slips are easy to miss during review, and they are
noticed late, when the code has already been merged.

Let's add the Gradle CheckStyle plugin, using the rule set from the
AddressBook Level 3 project because it is the configuration that
matches the SE-EDU Java coding standard. Wiring it into the build
means `gradlew check` fails on a violation, so style is enforced by
the build rather than by the reviewer.

The first run reported eight violations, fixed here:

* Parser declared its private constructor above the static
  constants. DeclarationOrder wants statics first, so the
  constructor moves below them.
* Four assertions in ParserTest wrapped so that a lambda's `(`
  opened the next line. SeparatorWrap wants a wrapped `(` to stay
  on the previous line, and each of these fits on one line within
  the 120-column limit anyway.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-CheckStyle into master
Add a GUI
commitResults.messageBody:
Ted only talks over a terminal, which means the app has to be started
from a command line and its replies scroll away with everything else
in the shell.

Let's give Ted a JavaFX window, built the way the SE-EDU tutorial
describes: the layout in FXML, the behaviour in a controller, and the
JavaFX libraries taken from Maven Central for all three OSes so the
jar is not tied to the machine that built it.

Ui no longer prints; it builds up a reply that flush() hands back.
That is what lets one chatbot serve both interfaces -- the terminal
prints the reply between its divider lines, and the window puts the
same text in a dialog box, where the dividers would be clutter. Ted
gains getResponse for the GUI to call a message at a time, while run()
keeps the text interface working, which is still the easier of the two
to test.

The entry point is a separate Launcher class. JavaFX will not start
from a class that extends Application when its libraries are on the
classpath rather than the module path, which is how this project
depends on them.

The bye command is kept rather than leaving the window close button as
the only way out, since quitting by typing matches the rest of the
app's command-driven feel. The window closes a moment after the
goodbye so the message can be read.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-Level-10 into master
Use varargs where the argument count varies
commitResults.messageBody:
Two places build up a result from a number of pieces that is fixed per
caller but differs between callers, and both spell that out by hand.

Each Task subclass assembles its own save line, repeating the escaping
and separator placement that the base class already knows how to do.
Let's replace toSavePrefix with toSaveLine(String...), so a subclass
names only the fields it adds -- none for a todo, by for a deadline,
from and to for an event -- and the escaping and separators stay in
one place.

Ui called show once per line, so a two-line reply read as two
unrelated statements. Let's make show take varargs, so each reply is
one call whose arguments are the lines the user will see.

Both are cases where the count varies by caller and every argument
means the same kind of thing, which is what varargs are for. Passing
an explicit array, or overloading for one and two extra fields, would
say the same thing with more ceremony.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-Varargs into master
Encapsulate task fields and fix stale comments
commitResults.messageBody:
Task, Deadline and Event keep their fields protected and mutable, and
TaskList reads a task's description straight from the field. Deadline
and Event each hold their own copy of the display date format.

Several comments no longer match the code. ExitCommand describes the
old conversation loop, Ui's show methods say they print, and
TaskList#asList says it returns a view when it returns a copy.
DialogBox catches a failed FXML load to keep the app running, yet the
next line fails with a NullPointerException anyway.

Fields that any class in the package can reassign undercut the
guarantees Task exists to give, and comments that contradict the code
mislead the next reader.

Let's
* make the task fields private, and final where they never change,
  with Task#getDescription() for the search to use
* move the display format into Task so both subclasses share one copy
* correct the stale comments and Javadoc
* rethrow a failed DialogBox load as an IllegalStateException, since
  the FXML ships in the JAR and a missing one means a broken build

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Fix option parsing and untrimmed GUI input
commitResults.messageBody:
Parser locates /by, /from and /to with indexOf, which also matches
them inside a word. "event lunch w/tom /from ... /to ..." is rejected
because the /to in "w/tom" is taken for the separator.

The GUI passes its text field to Ted#getResponse as typed, and only
the terminal trims input, so "  list" in the GUI is an unknown
command. A warning about the save file also appears above the welcome
banner, because the constructor queues it before the greeting exists.

The first two reject ordinary input, and all three show up in the
GUI, which is the version people use.

Let's
* accept an option only as a standalone word
* trim input in Ted#getResponse, where the terminal and the GUI meet,
  rather than in each front end
* hold the startup warnings back until getGreeting has shown the
  welcome
* add a regression test for each case

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Use streams where loops only filter, map or join
commitResults.messageBody:
Four loops walk a collection only to keep some of its elements, turn
each element into something else, or join the results into a string:
finding tasks by keyword, looking up a command by its keyword, listing
every keyword, and turning tasks into save lines. Each hides that
simple intent behind an accumulator or an index that the reader has to
trace.

Let's write these four as streams, which name the operation directly
(filter, findFirst, map, joining) and leave no accumulator to follow.

Loops where a stream would not read more simply stay as they are:
Storage.load also counts the lines it skips, decodeSaveField looks one
character ahead, Ui.showNumbered needs each task's position, and
Task.toSaveLine appends other fields around its loop.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Let tasks carry tags and save them
commitResults.messageBody:
A task holds only a description, a done flag and, for deadlines and
events, their dates. A user cannot label related tasks, e.g. all the
tasks for one module, except by repeating the label in every
description, where nothing treats it as a label.

Let's give every task a set of tags such as #fun, shown after the
description and saved as one extra field after the done flag. A task
without tags keeps exactly the line it had before, and a field only
counts as tags when every word in it is a valid tag, so existing save
files load unchanged.

A Tag record holds the rule for what a tag may be, letters and digits
compared in lower case, so the tasks, the save file and later the
parser share one definition. Allowing only letters and digits also
keeps a tag from ever containing the spaces or pipes the save format
relies on.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add tag and untag commands
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks can hold tags, but no command attaches or removes them, so every
task's tags stay empty.

Let's add the commands tag and untag, which take a task number and one
or more tags, e.g. tag 2 #fun #school. One TagCommand handles both,
the way MarkCommand covers mark and unmark, since the two differ only
in the direction of the change and the wording.

An untag naming a tag the task does not have is rejected before
anything changes, because it usually means a typo, and removing the
other tags anyway would leave the task half changed. Tagging a task
with a tag it already has is accepted, since the result is what the
user asked for.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Let find search by tag
commitResults.messageBody:
Tags now label tasks, but find searches descriptions only, so a tag
cannot be used to pick out the tasks it labels.

Let's treat a find keyword that starts with # as a tag, and show only
the tasks that have exactly that tag, so #fun does not match #funny.
Any other keyword searches descriptions as before.

The tag search is its own FindByTagCommand rather than a branch inside
FindCommand, because matching a whole tag is a different rule from
finding text inside a description.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Assert the assumptions the code relies on
commitResults.messageBody:
Several classes rely on a guarantee made elsewhere without saying so.
If a later change breaks one of these guarantees, the failure appears
far from its cause, as a confusing reply or a NullPointerException.

Let's state each assumption with an assert whose message names what
guarantees it:
* Parser.parse never sees blank input, as Ted skips it
* Storage.parseLine never sees a blank line, as load() skips them,
  and never reaches its default branch, as fieldCountFor accepts
  only T, D and E
* TaskList is never given null, as Storage.load() skips unreadable
  lines instead of adding null
* Ted always has a task list, as the constructor makes an empty one
  when loading fails
* MainWindow always has a Ted, as Main calls setTed before showing
  the window

Let's also enable assertions for gradle run, as Java ignores them by
default. Tests already run with assertions on.

Checks on user input stay as exceptions, because bad input is expected
and must be reported even with assertions off. For the same reason
there is no assert that an event ends after it starts: the parser
rejects such an event, but a hand-edited save file can still hold one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

master now has A-Assertions, which adds an assert at the top of

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge pull request #3 from trigg770/branch-C-Tagging
commitResults.messageBody: C-Tagging: Tag tasks and find them by tag

commitResults.messageTitle: Update README for the ted package and GUI
commitResults.messageBody:
The README still calls the project a template and tells the reader to
run src/main/java/Ted.java. That file moved to src/main/java/ted/ when
Ted was split into packages, and the GUI starts from ted.Launcher, not
Ted.main().

A new reader following the steps cannot find the file, and does not
learn that Ted has a GUI at all.

Let's describe Ted instead of the template, point the run step at the
new location, and add how to start the GUI.

commitResults.messageTitle: build.gradle: Bundle JavaFX for Apple Silicon Macs
commitResults.messageBody:
Each JavaFX dependency uses the mac classifier, whose native libraries
are built for Intel Macs only. On an Apple Silicon Mac, a JDK without
JavaFX of its own cannot start Ted's window from the JAR.

Most Macs in use today are Apple Silicon.

Let's bundle the mac-aarch64 natives instead. The two Mac builds cannot
share one JAR, because their native libraries have the same file names.
A JDK that ships JavaFX, such as Zulu FX, uses its own copy either way.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Document test methods and tidy naming
commitResults.messageBody:
The coding standard asks for a Javadoc header on every non-private
method. JUnit test methods are public but have none, and neither does
Main.start(). A few local variables are named after their type (tasks,
taskList) rather than what they hold, and two comments use British
spelling while the rest of the code uses American.

Let's add the missing headers, rename those variables after their role
(loadedTasks, displayedTasks), and switch the two comments to American
spelling.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Handle more command format errors
commitResults.messageBody:
Parser reads a command only when it is spaced exactly as expected. A
double space or a tab between a date and its time makes the date
unreadable, and "List" typed with a capital, as phone keyboards do, is
an unknown command.

Other mistakes slip through: "list all" lists everything, a second /by
is read as part of the date, "delete 1 2" is reported as not a number,
and an event may end the moment it starts. A date that does not exist,
such as 30/2/2019, gets the same message as "tomorrow", which does not
tell the user which part to fix.

Let's
* read any run of spaces or tabs as one space, and command words in
  any case
* reject text after list and bye, a repeated /by, /from or /to, and
  more than one task number, each with its own message
* require an event to end after it starts
* tell a date that does not exist apart from one in the wrong format

The input is normalized once, at the top of parse(), so that no later
parsing step has to deal with spacing itself.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Reject duplicate tasks and redundant marks
commitResults.messageBody:
Adding a task that is already in the list stores a second copy.
Marking a task that is already done, or unmarking one that is not,
confirms a change that did not happen.

Duplicates leave the user unsure which copy to mark or delete, and a
false confirmation hides a mixed-up task number.

Let's report both as errors and leave the list unchanged. Two tasks
are duplicates when they are the same kind with the same description,
ignoring case, and for deadlines and events the same dates. The done
status and tags are not compared, as they change over a task's life
rather than describe the task.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep a copy of save files Ted cannot fully read
commitResults.messageBody:
When the save file has unreadable lines, Ted skips them, and its next
save writes only the tasks it could read, so those lines are lost. If
the whole file cannot be read, e.g. because it is not UTF-8 text, Ted
starts with an empty list and its next save wipes every task.

Some file errors are reported as just the file's path, as with a
permission error. If the window's layout fails to load, the app keeps
running with no window.

A hand-edited save file with one typo should not cost the user their
whole list.

Let's copy the file to ted.txt.bak before anything can overwrite it,
and say where the copy is in the greeting. Let's also explain common
file errors in plain words (permission denied, not UTF-8, a folder or
file in the wrong place), and close the app if its window cannot load.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-MoreErrorHandling'
commitResults.messageBody:
A-MoreErrorHandling: Handle more errors in input and the save file

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: build.gradle: Report test coverage with JaCoCo
commitResults.messageBody:
The tests pass, but nothing shows which parts of the code they never
run, so gaps in the tests go unnoticed.

Let's apply the JaCoCo plugin and have every test run write an HTML
and a CSV coverage report to build/reports/jacoco.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Skip save lines made only of separators
commitResults.messageBody:
Storage splits each line on " | " and reads the first field as the
task type. A line that is only " | " splits into no fields at all,
since split() drops trailing empty strings. Reading the first field
then throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, and Ted fails to start.

A hand-edited save file can easily end up with such a line.

Let's treat it as one more unreadable line, skipped and counted like
the others.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Number search results as in the full list
commitResults.messageBody:
find numbers its matches from 1, while mark, delete and tag take a
task's number in the full list. After "todo buy milk" and "todo read
book", "find book" shows read book as task 1, and "delete 1" then
deletes buy milk.

The number shown next to a task is the number the user types next, so
it must point at that task.

Let's number each match by its place in the full list. Tasks are looked
up by identity, so two tasks with the same description still get their
own numbers.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Show dates and search the same in every locale
commitResults.messageBody:
Dates are formatted, and search text lowered, using the computer's own
locale. On a Singapore English system, times show as "6:00 pm" rather
than "6:00 PM". On a Chinese system, the month and "PM" appear in
Chinese inside an English reply. On a Turkish system, "FINISH" lowers
to a word with a dotless i, so "find finish" misses "FINISH work".

Ted speaks English whatever the system settings, so its replies should
not change with them.

Let's format dates in English and fold case with Locale.ROOT, as Tag
already does. The tests now check the exact date text, which they
could not do while it varied by locale.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep the welcome banner lined up
commitResults.messageBody:
Ui.flush() strips the reply at both ends. The first line of the banner
starts with a space, which is removed, so the top row of the ASCII art
sits one column left of the rest.

Let's strip only trailing whitespace, which is all flush() promises to
remove.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Test the commands, Ui and the terminal loop
commitResults.messageBody:
DeleteCommand, ListCommand, ExitCommand and TagCommand are exercised
only indirectly, through ParserTest and TedTest. Ui's terminal methods
and Ted.run() have no tests at all. Coverage shows about 89% of the
non-GUI lines run, and under half of Ted's.

A-MoreTesting asks for tests covering nearly all code that can be
tested automatically.

Let's add tests for each command, CommandType, Ui and Ted's whole
conversation, including a restart and piped terminal input, and for
the file errors Storage now explains. Non-GUI line coverage rises to
98.6%. What remains is Ted.main() and the no-argument constructor,
which use the real save file, and one unreachable branch. The GUI
classes are tested by hand.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-MoreTesting'
commitResults.messageBody:
A-MoreTesting: Test nearly all non-GUI code and fix what it found

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Let the user scroll back through the conversation
commitResults.messageBody:
MainWindow keeps the newest message in view by binding the scroll
position to the height of the conversation. A bound property cannot be
set by anything else, so when the user drags the scroll bar or uses
the mouse wheel, JavaFX fails with "A bound value cannot be set" and
the view stays at the bottom.

Earlier replies, such as a list shown a few commands ago, are then out
of reach.

Let's move the scroll position to the bottom from a listener on the
conversation's height instead. New messages still scroll into view,
and the position stays free for the user to move.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Tell the GUI which messages report a problem
commitResults.messageBody:
Ted hands the GUI each reply as plain text. An error such as a mistyped
command looks just like a confirmation, so the GUI cannot show it any
differently.

A mistake the user does not notice leads them to think the command
worked.

Let's have Ted record whether its last message, reply or greeting,
explained a problem, and expose it through isError(), the same way
isExit() tells the GUI when to close. A greeting counts when it warns
about the save file.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Redesign the chat around a user talking to Ted
commitResults.messageBody:
Both sides of the conversation look the same: identical bubbles with a
large picture beside each, as if two people were chatting. The pictures
take up a quarter of the window's width, errors look like any other
reply, and the input box is a bare strip at the bottom. Fonts are given
as lists of fallbacks, but JavaFX uses only the first family in a list,
so Ted's replies lose their monospaced font where Menlo is missing, e.g.
on Windows, and the welcome banner breaks.

Ted's window takes up a small part of the screen, so space spent on
decoration is space taken from the replies.

Let's
* show the user's words in a solid bubble on the right with no picture,
  and Ted's replies on the left beside a small round picture
* show replies that explain a problem in red
* keep bubbles within 80% of the window's width, so the side a message
  is on stays obvious when the window is resized
* lay the window out with a BorderPane, so the input bar stretches with
  the window, and keep the focus in the input box after Send
* use JavaFX's logical System and Monospaced fonts, which exist on
  every platform

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-BetterGui'
commitResults.messageBody:
A-BetterGui: Redesign the chat window and fix scrolling

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Credit the JavaFX tutorial, Ted's picture and AI use
commitResults.messageBody:
Ted's GUI classes are adapted from the SE-EDU JavaFX tutorial, and
Ted's picture comes from Openclipart, but neither source is named
anywhere. Nor is the use of AI tools, which wrote much of the code.

The course's reuse policy counts uncredited reuse as plagiarism, and
asks for wide use of AI in the iP to be cited in the README.

Let's add an Acknowledgements section to the README naming the
tutorial, the picture's source and licence, and each AI tool with who
used it and what for. Let's also credit the tutorial in Main and
Launcher, as MainWindow and DialogBox already do.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: docs/README.md: Write the user guide
commitResults.messageBody:
The user guide is still the course's template, with placeholder
headings such as "Feature ABC".

It is the product website, so a new user has nothing to learn Ted's
commands from.

Let's describe how to install and start Ted, each command with its
format and an example reply taken from a real run, how saving works,
and a command summary table.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Give Ted the voice of a cheeky teddy bear
commitResults.messageBody:
Ted's replies are the course's example wording: "Got it. I've added
this task", "Noted", "Bye. Hope to see you again soon!". The greeting
opens with ASCII art of the name. Nothing in them says who Ted is, and
some read oddly, such as "Pick a number between 1 and 1".

A-Personality asks for a personality that shows in the chatbot's
phrases, not only its name.

Let's make Ted a cheeky teddy bear who teases the user a little but
always gets the job done:
* every confirmation, the greeting and the goodbye are in his voice,
  and the ASCII banner is dropped for a spoken introduction
* the task count comes with a remark that suits the size of the list
* every error keeps its explanation and ends with "Try:" and a working
  example, so the joke never hides how to fix the mistake

The wording avoids slang and idioms, as A-Personality asks, so that
classmates who are not native speakers can follow it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Dress Ted's window in teddy bear colors
commitResults.messageBody:
Ted now talks like a teddy bear, but his window is the same cool blue
and grey as before, and his replies are in a monospaced font chosen
only for the ASCII banner, which is gone.

A-Personality asks for the GUI to match the personality as well as
the words.

Let's
* color the window like a well-loved teddy bear: cream background,
  plush brown for the Send button and focused input, faded denim for
  the user's messages, with warm reds for errors
* show Ted's replies in the System font, which is easier to read
* round the bubbles and input box a little more
* use Ted's picture as the window icon, and prompt the user with
  "Tell Ted what to do..."

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Update the guide and screenshot for Ted's new voice
commitResults.messageBody:
The user guide's example replies, the README's sample output and
docs/Ui.png all show Ted as he was before A-Personality: the old
wording, the ASCII banner and the blue window.

A user comparing the guide with the app would see different replies
from the ones documented.

Let's replace each example with Ted's reply from a real run, introduce
Ted as a cheeky teddy bear, show what a red error reply looks like,
and retake the screenshot in the new colors.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Main: Correct the comment on the window icon
commitResults.messageBody:
The comment above the window icon says macOS shows its own icon for
Java apps instead. On macOS, Ted's picture does appear beside the
window title, so the comment misleads anyone reading why the icon is
set.

Let's describe where the icon appears without the wrong claim.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Let Ted remark on tasks set for 4:20
commitResults.messageBody:
Ted's personality shows in how he words each reply, but he has no
running joke of his own, nothing a user discovers by chance.

A small surprise makes a character feel more alive than one more
witty confirmation.

Let's give Ted a soft spot for 4:20, like the teddy bear in the film
he shares a name with. When a deadline or event added is due at, or
starts or ends at, 4:20 in the morning or afternoon, he says so. Each
kind of task reports whether one of its own times falls at a given
time of day, so Ui need not know which kinds have dates.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Reword two of Ted's lines
commitResults.messageBody:
Ted says "That event is over before it begins" when an event's end is
not after its start. It reads awkwardly, and does not fit an end that
equals the start. His reply to a search with no matches is plain next
to the rest of his voice.

Let's
* say "Even a bear knows the end comes after the start", which fits
  both cases and his being a bear
* have him find some snacks while searching under the sofa

Let's also update the user guide's example and the screenshot, which
show the old event line.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'branch-A-Personality'
commitResults.messageBody:
A-Personality: Make Ted a cheeky teddy bear

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Complete the credits the reuse policy asks for
commitResults.messageBody:
The README's Acknowledgements name the JavaFX tutorial, Ted's picture
and the AI tools used, but leave out the libraries Ted depends on and
the picture's artist. The user guide shows the picture in its
screenshot without crediting it, and follows the layout of the
AddressBook-Level3 user guide without saying so. The note on AI use
says what each tool did, but not how much of the project came from it.

The course's reuse policy asks for libraries to be listed in the
README, media to be credited where they first appear, and the extent
of AI use to be stated.

Let's list JavaFX, JUnit and the build plugins, credit the picture to
Machovka both in the README and under the screenshot, and credit the
AddressBook-Level3 user guide's layout. Let's also state how widely
Claude Code and Codex were used, as found in the saved sessions of
both tools, and what trigg770 did directly: directing the work,
writing some of the code, coming up with Ted's personality, and
reviewing the code.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Correct comments left stale by recent changes
commitResults.messageBody:
Several comments no longer match the code. The ted package calls Ted a
command-line task list and leaves the GUI classes out of its list. Ted
is described as the entry point, though the window starts from
Launcher, and its feature list stops at delete. A field comment
mentions the welcome banner, which is gone. Ui's class comment says all
wording lives in Ui, then says error messages do not. BUSY_TASK_COUNT
says "beyond" ten tasks where the code means ten or more. Parser still
explains that runs of spaces between tags do not matter, which parse()
now handles for every command.

Comments that disagree with the code mislead the next reader more than
missing ones do.

Let's bring each comment in line with what the code does now, and split
tag commands on the single spaces parse() leaves behind.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Tidy dashes in comments and test Javadoc tags
commitResults.messageBody:
Three comments use a double hyphen as a dash, which reads as a typo in
plain text. The Javadoc tags in TedTest and ParserTest start their
descriptions with a capital letter, while the main code starts them in
lower case.

Let's use a colon or brackets in place of the dashes, and describe the
test tags in lower case, as the rest of the code does.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Document the constructors of the GUI classes
commitResults.messageBody:
Launcher, Main and MainWindow rely on the constructor Java adds by
default, so the generated Javadoc warns that they have no comment. The
other classes all declare and document their constructors.

Main and MainWindow are created by JavaFX and FXMLLoader rather than by
Ted's own code, which a reader cannot tell from an implicit
constructor.

Let's declare each one with a comment saying who creates it: a private
constructor for Launcher, which is never created, and public ones for
Main and MainWindow, which JavaFX needs.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: build.gradle: Allow native access in the JAR
commitResults.messageBody:
Run on a JDK without JavaFX, the JAR's own JavaFX loads its native
libraries, and Java 25 prints four lines starting "WARNING: A
restricted method in java.lang.System has been called" before Ted's
window opens.

To a grader or first-time user, those lines look like something has
gone wrong.

Let's declare Enable-Native-Access: ALL-UNNAMED in the manifest, which
grants the access for code on the class path and removes those lines.
JavaFX's own warning about running from the class path remains, as the
manifest cannot affect it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: README: Link to the latest release and user guide
commitResults.messageBody:
The README explains how to set up Ted's code in IntelliJ, but a visitor
who only wants to use Ted finds no link to the JAR or to the user
guide.

Let's point to both at the top, using the releases/latest address so
the link stays correct after each new release.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
